sources.rank_basis: typescriptlang.org/docs/ is the TypeScript project's own official documentation site.
developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/ is MDN Web Docs, listed as authoritative secondary (Rank 3); it is not the ECMAScript spec.
v8.dev/blog/ is the V8 engineering blog, named in the Rank 4 row; it could also be read as the project's own publication (Rank 1), so the higher number applies.
nodejs.org/api/ is the Node.js project's official API documentation (cached copy is the v26.13.1 docs, with a version-history table).

sources.url: Worked example measurement (Node 24.22 / V8 13.6, 2026-10-25) and Node 24.22 re-tests (2026-11-03)
sources.rank_basis: Author's own experiment; not cited as a footnote and not carrying any ✅.

claim_checks.claim: `private` and `protected` are enforced only during type checking. Runtime lookups, and bracket notation even during type checking, still reach the member: it is "soft private".
claim_checks.page_says: private and protected are only enforced during type checking. ... private also allows access using bracket notation during type checking ... these fields are soft private
claim_checks.note: The first sentence and the runtime-lookup part hold for both modifiers. The page gives the bracket-notation escape and the 'soft private' label to `private` only; the doc's sentence extends them to `protected` members too (wider scope).

claim_checks.claim: `#` fields stay private after compilation and have no bracket-notation escape hatch: they are "hard private".
claim_checks.page_says: JavaScript’s private fields (#) remain private after compilation and do not provide the previously mentioned escape hatches like bracket notation access, making them hard private.

claim_checks.claim: When compiling to ES2021 or lower, TypeScript replaces `#` with `WeakMap`s. The handbook notes that these runtime privacy checks could affect performance.
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #. ... Note that these added privacy checks during runtime could affect performance.
claim_checks.note: Both parts match, and 'could' is kept. The handbook's performance note covers closures, WeakMaps and private fields alike; the doc applies it to the WeakMap output only (see the Summary violation).

claim_checks.claim: Private elements are not properties. They cannot be enumerated, deleted, proxied, or reached through `Object` methods, and `structuredClone()` does not copy them.
claim_checks.page_says: they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method. ... structuredClone() does not clone private elements
claim_checks.note: 'Not properties' matches MDN's note that a property has a string or symbol key and attributes, and private elements have none.

claim_checks.claim: Reading a `#` field from an object whose class did not declare it throws a `TypeError`. `#x in obj` checks for it without throwing.
claim_checks.page_says: If you access a private element from an object that doesn't have the element, a TypeError is thrown ... return true if the private field or method exists, and false otherwise
claim_checks.note: The doc's condition wording is the error message MDN prints for C.getX({}): 'Cannot read private member #x from an object whose class did not declare it'.

claim_checks.claim: V8 9.7 moved class-field initialization, including private fields, onto its inline-cache fast path. Before that it went through slower runtime calls.
claim_checks.page_says: With v9.7, when V8 considers the pattern of the initialization to be predictable enough, it uses a new IC to speed up the operation
claim_checks.note: The version and the 'before: costly runtime call' part match. The doc drops the condition: the fast path applies only when the pattern is predictable, and the page says the IC still falls back to the runtime for proxies, a field that already exists, or an unseen hidden class.

claim_checks.claim: Private elements cannot be proxied [row: Object wrapped in a `Proxy` | `#` access does not go through the proxy]
claim_checks.page_says: While private elements are accessed with the familiar dot notation, they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method.
claim_checks.note: The Why cell matches. The row's 'What happens' cell is vague; see the structure violation for this row.

claim_checks.claim: TypeScript downlevels it [row: Target ES2021 or lower | `#` becomes `WeakMap` lookups]
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #.

claim_checks.claim: So code meant to run unbuilt keeps injected collaborators as `readonly #field`s assigned in the constructor [row: Working around it with `--experimental-transform-types` | Runs on Node 24.22 with an `ExperimentalWarning` (re-tested 2026-11-03); the flag is removed in Node 26.0.0]
claim_checks.page_says: not found (searched: readonly, private, collaborat, #field, unbuilt). The page does say: "Removed --experimental-transform-types flag." (v26.0.0) and lists "parameter properties" among unsupported features.
claim_checks.note: The ✅ closes the doc's own design recommendation, which [^4] does not state. The row's premises are on the page (flag removed in v26.0.0; parameter properties need transformation), so the mark belongs on the 'What happens' cell.

claim_checks.claim: Node only deletes types [row: Type stripping itself | Stable (stability 2) since Node 24.12.0 and 25.2.0; no warning since 24.3.0; Node ignores `tsconfig.json` and needs `.ts` extensions in relative imports]
claim_checks.page_says: Since Node.js is only removing inline types, any TypeScript features that involve replacing TypeScript syntax with new JavaScript syntax will error.
claim_checks.note: The context cell's versions, the stability index, tsconfig being ignored and mandatory file extensions also match the page's history table and text.

conflicts.topic: Runtime cost of hard privacy (`#` fields)
conflicts.winner: [^1] rank 1 (hedged: hard-privacy checks, private fields included, 'could affect performance')
conflicts.loser: local measurement, rank local (Summary: '# fields costs the same as public fields' on any native ES2022+ target; Takeaways: 'measured cost is nil')

violations.evidence: C1: item 1 extends bracket-notation access and the 'soft private' label to `protected`; [^1] gives both to `private` only ('private also allows access using bracket notation during type checking').

C6: item 6 says V8 9.7 moved class-field initialization onto the IC fast path with no condition; [^3] says it does so only 'when V8 considers the pattern of the initialization to be predictable enough', and falls back to the runtime otherwise.

C9: the ✅[^4] closes the recommendation 'keeps injected collaborators as readonly #fields'; [^4] has nothing on it. It supports only the row's premises (flag removed in v26.0.0; parameter properties unsupported).

Proxy row: '# access does not go through the proxy' leaves out the real failure. A method called through the proxy reads this.#x on the proxy object, which lacks the element, so it throws TypeError ([^2]: 'cannot be proxied' plus 'If you access a private element from an object that doesn't have the element, a TypeError is thrown').

The TL;DR states as fact that '# fields costs the same as public fields' on any 'native ES2022+ target', and Takeaways says 'measured cost is nil'. Neither carries ✅ or ⚠️. The only evidence is one local run on V8 13.6 plus [^3] (V8 only, and only for predictable patterns). How it works 3 also limits the rank-1 handbook caveat to the WeakMap output, while [^1] applies it to private fields too. No cached source contradicts the measurement, so this is not a KB-17 failure, but the claim reaches further than its evidence.

The 'Where each form fits' table is a decision guide (role 6 content) inside the mechanism section. It overlaps the ## Trade-offs table and holds an uncited, unmarked fact (TS18009). This is the one weak section behind diataxis_rigor 4.
